https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/scie.text: Dog parents, this is your âtold youâ moment! All those times you felt your dog sensed your mood before you even said a word, that wasn't nothing. The time when you were crying your heart out and your baby just rested on your lap? That was him reading you. Not guessing. Not just picking up on body language or the sound of your voice, though he really knew what you were going through. He may not know the reason, but he knew you were sad and needed love. Not just in sadness, he knew how ecstatic you were when you landed your first job. And also, the time you were scared and he refused to leave your side? Your buddy knew that too.Scientists have finally begun to understand whatâs going on inside your dog's brain and confirmed what you already knew! Dogs don't just notice when you're upset. They can tell the difference between sadness, fear and anger. A new study published in the Cell Press journal iScience found that dogs can distinguish between human emotions such as laughs, frowns and tears. And the best part: dogs process smiles in a unique brain region!Smile at your dog; they love it!For the first time, scientists have evidence suggesting that dogs can distinguish between negative facial expressions, including anger, sadness and fear. âHumans are really good at picking up small details on the face, and so are dogs. This makes dogs very interesting. By studying their brains, we can understand what adaptations have developed to support their remarkable social and emotional understanding of humans,â first author RaÃºl HernÃ¡ndez-PÃ©rez from the University of Vienna said.The researchers initially focused on happiness, the expression which had a particular significance for dogs, according to previous studies. To understand whatâs going on in their brains, the researchers scanned eight dogs. During the scan, the dogs were shown images of strangers with either happy or neutral expressions. And guess what? Every time they were shown happy faces, the temporal cortex and the caudate nucleus, the regions in dogsâ brains linked to higher cognitive and reward processing, respectively, lit up!âThe activity in the caudate nucleus is particularly interesting. It suggests that happy human faces may have emotional significance for dogs,â Laura Cuaya, also of the University of Vienna, who began the research at the National Autonomous University of Mexico and later expanded it through a collaboration at EÃ¶tvÃ¶s LorÃ¡nd University in Hungary, explained.Your dog understands your emotionsThe researchers also wanted to understand if the same regions of the brain respond to other emotions. So they showed images of people displaying happiness, anger, fear and sadness to 12 dogs. Using machine learning, the researchers analysed their brain activity. What the researchers found was striking. The dogs did not react the same way to these negative emotions. The temporal cortex-caudate nucleus network of dogs reacted uniquely to happiness. This means they are able to distinguish smiles from all three negative expressions. However, the dogs did not merely sort the world into good and bad, researchers said.Another brain analysis found that there were distinct patterns of activity in how they separated fear from anger and sadness. This is the first time scientists have found evidence suggesting dogs can distinguish between specific negative facial expressions. They can tell if you are sad or frightened.Understanding an emotion doesnât mean they experience it like usThough dogs can distinguish between these emotions, it does not mean that they experience emotions exactly the same way humans do, researchers said. Also, a still photo of a human face doesnât tell the whole story; in real life, dogs watch human body language, listen to nuances in our voices and detect information from our scent.âWhen we compare humans with primates, we are looking at abilities that may have come from a common ancestor. With dogs, the story is totally different. They followed a very different evolutionary path, yet through domestication, they developed the social abilities needed to understand and cooperate with us,â senior author Laura Cuaya of the University of Vienna said.The study only included pets who had loving families. The researchers noted that free-ranging dogs, like the ones who live on the street, navigate in a different social environment, which also means they may process human cues differently.The researchers are now hoping to understand how dogs integrate these brain signals to make sense of the humans around them. They also plan to compare how human and dog brains process the same emotional signals.âI would like people to see dogs as emotional beings. They have evolved with us to understand our expressions and cooperate with us, and recognising that can change how we communicate with and care for them,â Cuaya added.

https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world.text: Russian strikes on Ukraine killed at least two people overnight into Sunday, officials said, hours after Moscow rejected German calls to ease off its escalation toward NATO. Russia’s top diplomat on Saturday brushed off what’s believed to have been the first tête-à-tête with his German counterpart since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The meeting was held during the UN General Assembly’s annual gathering of world leaders, as an intensifying aerial war between Russia and Ukraine shows no sign of slowing. Ties between Russia and Germany have soured in recent weeks, following an attempted drone attack last month at Leipzig airport that Berlin blamed on the Kremlin. With front-line positions largely unchanged since last year, Moscow has hammered its neighbour with cruise and ballistic missiles, powerful glide bombs and jet-powered drones in recent months. Meanwhile, Kyiv’s long-range drones have targeted Russian oil refineries and businesses. In Kyiv, a man was found dead after a Russian drone hit a non-residential building overnight, according to Ukraine’s emergency service. Another drone struck a single-story vehicle repair shop, leaving firefighters battling the blaze into early Sunday, the emergency service said. Russian forces also struck Ukraine’s southern Odesa region, which surrounds the country’s main Black Sea port, multiple times overnight into Sunday, killing one person and injuring two others, according to the head of the local military administration, Oleh Kiper. In Russian-occupied Ukraine, a strike by Kyiv's forces on Sunday killed a civilian woman in Enerhodar, the town housing Europe's largest nuclear plant, according to its Kremlin-installed mayor. Maxim Pukhov said the Ukrainian drones also injured two others. Russia and Ukraine have repeatedly blamed each other for damaging power lines supplying Enerhodar's Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant, which Moscow captured early in the war. The plant is not in service, but needs power to keep cooling systems running and maintain safety.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwj3.text: Figure caption, Trump: US "had a threat" that led to withdrawal of bombers at RAF Fairford By Henry Moore Published 5 October 2026 President Donald Trump has said the US moved its bombers out of RAF Fairford because of "some threats" to the base. The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America. Speaking to reporters as he departed for Nebraska on Monday, Trump said the US had known of a "threat", which led them to move the bombers. Earlier on Monday, a No 10 spokesperson had insisted RAF Fairford was safe and pointed to Trump's comments last week, where he praised the UK's "police, defence and security services" in relation to the base. What prompted the US bombers to leave RAF Fairford? Published 6 hours ago What makes RAF Fairford one of the UK's most important military sites? Published 6 days ago Trump's comments appear to confirm reports by US media that a new threat led to the bombers being removed after a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase. While speaking to a gaggle of reporters outside the White House, Trump was asked if a "specific threat" had led the US to pull its bombers from the airbase. Trump replied: "Yeah I think we can say that. They didn't fly out by accident. "There were some threats. And rather than tempting the enemy, we'll capture the enemy and beat the enemy. But why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit. Not very far." He added Washington "actually knows the people that made the threat", but he did not confirm who. The exact nature of the threat that prompted the aircraft's removal from RAF Fairford remains unclear, but sources in Washington speculated to the BBC it might have revolved around sabotage attempts or attempts to strike the sensitive, expensive aircraft in the event of resumed hostilities with Iran. One source close to the White House pointed to Ukraine's Operation Spiderweb - a covert drone attack on five Russian bases in June last year - as an example of what an enemy force could do, even at a distance. "Whatever they thought it was, it was taken extremely seriously," the source said. Trump's comments, and those of Vance before him, stand in stark contrast to those of Secretary of State Marco Rubio. While both Trump and Vance pointed to an unspecified threat, Rubio was much more guarded in his language, noting that it was "not unusual" for military units and assets to rotate and be moved around the world. RAF Fairford - in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire - has been at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter-terror police. Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences and subsequently released on bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail. Following the release of the first five men , Trump criticised the decision and US officials suggested Iran could have been involved in the incident. Whitehall sources have not disputed that the decision from Washington to remove the bombers was in response to the incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire. Speaking earlier on Monday, Rubio said he would not directly tie last week's incident to the decision to pull bombers from RAF Fairford. He added: "It's not unusual to see movement of assets to different parts of the world based on exercises, redeployments, people changing out and new people coming in, new planes coming in and old planes going out." Rubio said the US still had full confidence in the security of all its bases and that British authorities had been very co-operative since the incident. Vance later said the bombers had been moved out of an "abundance of caution", adding Washington felt Iran was doing what it had "done for 49 years... which is engage in acts of terrorism against the US and against a lot of other people". Days after the incident at RAF Fairford, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident but he did not provide further details, while Rubio said it had "clearly involve[d] the hands of a foreign actor" without going into further details. Tehran has strongly denied any involvement. In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces". RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford, has been used as a forward operating location by the US air force for decades. In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran. The redeployment from RAF Fairford will reduce America's capacity to "quickly surge sorties against Iran, reducing the threat level somewhat", Christoph Bergs, research analyst at defence think tank the Royal United Services Institute told the Reuters news agency. However, the use of the base had already been limited given London's stipulation that it should only be used for defensive strikes, he added. The planes could potentially be sent to either Diego Garcia or bases in the Gulf to reduce the need for air-to-air refuelling but that would depend on capacity availability, negotiations with allies and security, Bergs added. https://www.heraldmalaysia.com/news/paro.text: Read Herald PDF in Chinese English Malay Tamil Synod Malaysian Church News In Malay Global Church Editorial Multimedia Spiritual Resources Parolin: Totalitarian regimes of past defeated; temptation to 'be like God' remains Cardinal Secretary of State Pietro Parolin delivers the opening address at the Pontifical Gregorian University’s international academic conference, “The Holy See and Totalitarian Systems in the 20th Century: New Perspectives and Research Approaches,” warning that there are still those who seek to “control how humanity lives and thinks." Oct 29, 2026 Related News Pope in Peru: ‘Distance does not necessarily diminish love for one’s homeland’ As Pope Leo visits Peru, young people welcome new reasons to hope Argentina's next task: Turn Pope Leo's words into action Pope at Mass in Argentina: Mission is a ‘joyful duty’ Pope to Argentine young people: ‘Who told you it was too late?’ Pope Leo XIV’s third day in Argentina Cardinal Parolin delivers his address at the Gregorian University By Alessandro Di Bussolo Although the totalitarian regimes of the past, such as National Socialism, communism, and fascism, now belong to history, “the phenomenon itself does not: it arises from the human temptation to want to ‘be like God,’ to control how humanity lives and thinks, and to impose one’s own ideological convictions on it.” Cardinal Secretary of State Pietro Parolin emphasized this in his opening address on October 28, at the international academic conference in the main hall of the Pontifical Gregorian University. Organized by the Gregorian University and the Pontifical Committee for Historical Sciences, the conference continues until October 29. Pope Leo XIV and Magnifica humanitas The harm caused by this human temptation to “want to be like God,” symbolized by the biblical Tower of Babel, was also highlighted by Pope Leo XIV in his encyclical Magnifica humanitas . As Cardinal Parolin recalled, freedom and democracy do not rest on “rules and procedures alone,” but on “a solid concordance with the facts and a genuine commitment to the good of individuals and society as a whole,” and therefore on “fidelity to the truth.” Holy See from Pius XI to Saint John Paul II In his address, the Vatican Secretary of State traced the Holy See’s position toward twentieth-century totalitarian systems during the pontificates from Pius XI to Saint John Paul II. He examined the emergence of totalitarian regimes “that promised to bring about a social utopia in this world,” fueled by secularism, which “had excluded religion from the public sphere, no longer recognized God as the center and supreme authority of history, and put human beings in his place.” Totalitarian regimes as “political religions” “By elevating social class, race, or the state to the altar in God’s place,” the Cardinal recalled, these regimes “sacralized their ideological concepts and created political religions, with their own ‘liturgies,’ prophets, martyrs, and ethical norms that dissolved the human person into an all-encompassing collective.” Pseudo-religious ideologies such as communism and National Socialism, he stressed, “were irreconcilably opposed to Christianity and unleashed a wave of persecution against the Catholic Church from the outset.” Seeking “the path of negotiation” In an effort to protect European Catholics living under these regimes, Pope Pius XI initially chose “the path of negotiation”: with the Soviet Union, Fascist Italy through the Lateran Pacts, and Nazi Germany through the Concordat. The relationship continued only with Italy, but these were nevertheless fragile relations with partners “subservient to ideologies hostile to Christianity.” In March 1937, Pius XI therefore issued three encyclical letters “that condemned National Socialism, communism, and the anti-Catholic liberal-socialist regime in Mexico.” According to Cardinal Parolin, the Pope clearly expressed “that all these heretical deviations stemmed from the same materialism which, by denying God, claimed to bring a new salvation to the world through revolutionary human means.” Pius XII and Summi Pontificatus His successor, Pius XII, maintained this fundamental outlook. In his first encyclical, Summi Pontificatus , issued at the outbreak of the Second World War, he denounced the ultimate roots of the conflict as lying “in society’s departure from the teaching of Christ, which had once given Europe spiritual cohesion, in the neglect of natural law, and in the rejection of a universal standard of morality.” Only a return to God “and to an order centered on Christian values” could restore humanity to genuine peace founded on justice and equity. Pacelli’s vision for the postwar world After attempts to mediate peace between the warring parties had failed, Pope Pius XII launched “a diplomacy of charity on an unprecedented scale,” Cardinal Parolin recalled, to assist persecuted and needy people “of every background.” He also developed “a blueprint for the postwar world that would ensure a just and lasting peace, rooted in Christian inspiration and based on international solidarity and respect for the dignity and natural rights of individuals and nations, including small nations and those that had been defeated.” He condemned the unspeakable crimes of the war, but did so in a way “that would not provoke even greater persecution.” Failed efforts to reach an agreement with “people’s democracies” Cardinal Parolin stressed that Pius XII’s resolute anti-communism did not prevent him, after the war, from seeking an agreement with the “people’s democracies” to ease the suffering of persecuted Catholics. He sought to negotiate with Czechoslovakia, Hungary, and Poland. It was the communist regimes, however, that broke off all dialogue, including through the conviction of Cardinal József Mindszenty in Hungary and the launch of a schismatic “Catholic Action” in Czechoslovakia. This led to the decrees of excommunication issued between 1949 and 1951, through which he condemned any collaboration with communist ideology, while expressing spiritual and practical solidarity with the “Church of Silence.” An era of dialogue, from Saint John XXIII to Saint Paul VI Turning to the subsequent period, Cardinal Parolin explained that “the new approach of ‘dialogue’ with the countries of Eastern Europe in the rigid climate of the Cold War undoubtedly represented one of the most complex aspects of the Holy See’s diplomatic activity during the pontificates of John XXIII and Paul VI.” Both Popes, but especially Pope Paul VI, pursued dialogue and détente “with the primary aim of giving the Catholic Church in that part of Europe greater room to live and operate,” aware that communist political regimes would endure for a long time. The Catholic Church could thus act as a “moral force,” autonomous and independent of the logic of the two blocs. Vatican Ostpolitik and international détente This was what came to be known as “Vatican Ostpolitik ,” whose primary objective “was religious rather than political, although achieving it required the traditional instruments of politics and diplomacy.” Cardinal Agostino Casaroli was the chief architect of this dialogue, facing the dilemma of whether to “resist or negotiate.” In 1965, the Secretary of State recalled, Paul VI said that “the Holy See refrains from raising its legitimate voice of protest and disapproval more frequently and forcefully” in defense of the suffering Church “in countries with atheist and totalitarian regimes,” so as “not to provoke greater evils.” The Holy See’s policy toward the East, Cardinal Parolin said, “would contribute substantially to international détente.” Despite its limited success, “that choice was right, according to the unanimous judgment of historians.” Saint John Paul II and the fall of the Wall Finally, Cardinal Parolin turned to John Paul II, the Pope associated with the “fall of the Wall.” He did not halt negotiations with Eastern Europe but, “convinced of the weakness of communist regimes,” focused his energies “on mobilizing Christian consciences, strengthening the historical and cultural identity of Europe’s peoples, rooted in Christianity, and renewing the unity of the continent, which needed once again to breathe with both lungs.” His goal was not simply the fall of communism, “but rather the re-Christianization of the peoples of Europe.” This hope, the Secretary of State concluded, “nevertheless remained unfulfilled.” -- Vatican News Total Comments: 0 Spiritual Resources Saint of the Day St. Josaphat First Reading Philemon 7-20 Psalm Psalms 146:7-10 Gospel Luke 17:20-25 Shalom Lord, help me be aware
